newsitem.title: USA: USDA seen hiking soy stocks despite exports, crush.
newsitem.headline: USDA seen hiking soy stocks despite exports, crush.

text.p: Record large weekly soybean exports and historically high crushing rates have increased U.S. soybean usage but Tuesday's U.S. Agriculture Department ending stocks figures will likely be higher, analysts said.

"I think USDA will be conservative," said Everen Securities analyst Joel Karlin, referring to Tuesday's USDA crop reports. "I think USDA is going to increase production, but (apply) half of it to stocks and half to usage."
A pre-report survey indicated that analysts expect USDA to increase its soybean production figure by 30 million bushels to 2.376 billion bushels.
The crop report is due on Tuesday at 0730 CST/1330 GMT.
Karlin and other analysts said USDA has been slow to raise usage figures in the past.

USDA put ending soybean stocks at 195 million bushels on the October crop report. Karlin said he expected that number to increase to 234 million bushels, a reflection of both a larger production estimate and a smaller increase in usage.

Strong demand in October for soybeans pushed U.S. weekly export figures to record highs. As of October 31, U.S. soybean export sales totaled 11.23 million tonnes for the marketing year which began October 1.
That figure stood at 9.687 million tonnes at the same point last year, USDA said.

High crush margins and continued strong domestic and export demand supported weekly soybean crush levels as well. The crush stood at 29.90 million bushels in the week ended November 6 versus 27.98 million for the same week last year, the National Oilseed Processors Association said.
But despite strong demand during October, analysts said usage figures would likely increase by only about half as much as production figures rise.

"USDA will lag on the usage figures," said Dave Armstrong, analyst with The Chicago Corporation. "If they go up 50 million (bushels) on the crop production, they'll go up 20 or 25 (million bushels) in the stocks."
Analysts noted USDA raised its export demand figure on the October report, due largely to a pickup in sales to China.
"They were fairly aggressive with the export number last month," Armstrong said. "I don't see them going to 900 (million bushels) this time just because we had a good month of export."
USDA in October pegged export demand at 850 million bushels, up from 815 million the previous month.

The export data reflected an active period in October when harvest pressure drove markets to seasonal lows, said Harry Baumes, senior vice-president for agriculture at the WEFA Group, a Philadelphia-based consulting firm.

"We can't expect to see this pace of exports throughout the year," Baumes said. "Some of the countries that we're shipping to may be perceiving that we're at harvest lows. There's a lot of months left in the crop year."
